# Table 1: the rank gradient in cooperation

## What we want to measure

Take one decision: child $i$ meets classmate $j$. Two things describe the
pair:

- the **Social Rank GAP**, $\text{Rank}_i - \text{Rank}_j$, between $-1$ and
  $1$. It is positive when $i$ is the higher-ranked child of the two;
- the **Cooperation GAP**, tokens $i$ received from $j$ minus tokens $i$
  sent to $j$, between $-10$ and $10$. It is positive when $i$ came out
  ahead.

If cooperation were blind to rank, the Cooperation GAP would be unrelated to
the rank gap. If lower-ranked children give more to higher-ranked
classmates than they get back, the Cooperation GAP rises with the rank gap.
The slope of that relation is the quantity of interest.

Each pair appears twice in the data, once from each side, with both gaps
changing sign. This is what we want: every child is a sender in some rows,
and the model compares the same sender across her different partners.

## The model

For a decision of sender $i$ toward partner $j$, in classroom $c$ and round $t$:

$$
\text{Coop GAP}_{ijct} = \beta\, \text{RankGAP}_{ij} + \eta_i + \kappa_{c \times t} + u_{ijct}
$$

Each term has a job:

- $\eta_i$, **sender fixed effects**. Some children are generous with
  everyone, others with no one. The sender fixed effect absorbs each child's
  own level, so $\beta$ is estimated only from how the *same* child's
  exchanges differ across her partners.
- $\kappa_{c\times t}$, **classroom-by-round fixed effects**. A classroom
  may be more cooperative overall, and giving may drift during the session.
  These fixed effects compare only decisions made in the same classroom and
  round, the unit within which partners were drawn at random.
- **Standard errors clustered by classroom.** Decisions from the same
  classroom share children, teachers and nomination networks, so they are
  not independent. Clustering by classroom (45 clusters) allows for any
  correlation within a classroom.

Because partners were assigned at random within each classroom and round,
the rank of the partner a child met is unrelated to her own characteristics
(Figure 1D below checks this). So $\beta$ can be read as how the same child's
exchanges change when she happens to meet a higher- or lower-ranked
classmate.

The model is estimated separately in five samples, one per column of Table 1:
all pairs, non-friends, mutual friends, and the two kinds of one-sided
friendships, seen from the side of the child who named the other: a
lower-ranked child naming a higher-ranked one (L→H) or the reverse (H→L).

```{r table1-packages}
```

```{r table1-samples}
```

The two one-sided samples are small (fewer than 1,000 decisions each, and
few decisions per classroom and round), so they use classroom fixed effects
instead of classroom-by-round fixed effects.

The function `felm()` from the package **lfe** estimates linear models with
many fixed effects. Its formula has four parts separated by `|`: the
regression, the fixed effects, instruments (none here, `0`) and the
variable that defines the clusters.

```{r table1-models}
```

## Panel B: effects in more intuitive units

A slope of $\beta$ tokens per unit of rank gap is hard to picture, because a
full unit (from the bottom to the top of a classroom) is rare. Panel B
expresses the same estimate in three other ways:

- **in tokens**, for a typical difference in rank (one standard deviation of
  the Social Rank GAP);
- **in standard deviations of the Cooperation GAP**, which makes the effect
  comparable across samples;
- **model-adjusted**, using only the variation in the rank gap that remains
  after removing the fixed effects. This is the variation the model actually
  uses, so this number is the most conservative of the three.

```{r table1-panel-b}
```

## Regression results {#the-table}

### Coefficient summary by sample

One row per sample, with the estimated slope, standard error, model fit, and effect sizes.

```{r table1-assemble}
```

### Table 1. Results in the manuscript layout

Each column corresponds to a sample. Standard errors are shown in parentheses.

```{r table1-display}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
b <- function(sample, what = "beta") table1[[what]][table1$sample == sample]
```

**How to read it.** Among non-friends, a one-unit increase in the Social Rank
GAP raises the Cooperation GAP by `r num(b("Non-friends"))` tokens
(SE `r num(b("Non-friends", "se"))`, P `r pval(b("Non-friends", "p_value"))`),
in favor of the higher-ranked child. Over the full range, from the lowest-
to the highest-ranked child of a classroom (a gap of 2), this is about
`r num(2 * b("Non-friends"), 1)` tokens out of 10. Among mutual friends the
slope is `r num(b("Mutual friends"))` and not distinguishable from zero.
The column with all pairs is close to the non-friends column, because
non-friends are 78% of the pairs.

In the one-sided friendships, the L→H slope (`r num(b("Asym. (L->H)"))`) looks
like the non-friend slope. The H→L estimate is imprecise
(SE `r num(b("Asym. (H->L)", "se"))`), as this sample is the smallest.

The $R^2$ is high in the small samples because the many fixed effects
explain much of the variation when each child contributes only a few
decisions; the adjusted $R^2$ corrects for the number of fixed effects.

## Is the slope flatter among mutual friends?

Separate regressions describe each group but do not test whether two slopes
differ. For that we pool non-friends and mutual friends in a single model
and let the slope change with friendship:

$$
\text{Coop GAP}_{ijct} = \beta_1 \text{RankGAP}_{ij} + \beta_2\, \text{Mutual}_{ij}
 + \beta_3 \,(\text{RankGAP}_{ij} \times \text{Mutual}_{ij}) + \eta_i + \kappa_{c\times t} + u_{ijct}
$$

$\beta_1$ is the slope among non-friends, and $\beta_1 + \beta_3$ the slope
among mutual friends. The test of interest is $\beta_3 = 0$.

```{r pooled-interaction}
```

```{r}
#| include: false
b3   <- pooled_table$Estimate[pooled_table$term == "rank_gap:mutual"]
b3_p <- pooled_table$`Pr(>|t|)`[pooled_table$term == "rank_gap:mutual"]
b1   <- pooled_table$Estimate[pooled_table$term == "rank_gap"]
```

The interaction is $\beta_3$ = `r num(b3, 3)` (P `r pval(b3_p)`): among
mutual friends the rank gradient is `r num(b1 + b3)` tokens instead of
`r num(b1)`, a reduction of about `r round(100 * -b3 / b1)`%. The level
difference $\beta_2$ is close to zero. This is expected: the two decisions of
a pair have Cooperation GAPs of opposite sign, so a characteristic shared by
both children of the pair, such as being mutual friends, can hardly shift the
level of the Cooperation GAP; what it can change is the slope.

```{r table1-save}
```

# Figure 1D: was partner rank really random?

The interpretation of Table 1 rests on random assignment: which classmate a
child met in a round should not depend on who the child is. Here we check
this for three characteristics of the sender: sex, attendance and grade
point average (GPA).

One detail matters. In a given round a child can only be paired with the
other children who play in that round. So the benchmark is not the average
rank of the whole classroom but the average rank of the *other* active
children in that classroom and round. The outcome is the partner's rank
minus that benchmark: positive means the child met a partner of higher rank
than expected by chance.

```{r balance-packages}
```

```{r balance-data}
```

```{r expected-partner-rank}
```

We then regress that outcome on the sender's characteristics, with
classroom-by-round fixed effects and standard errors clustered by
classroom. If assignment is random, all coefficients should be close to
zero.

```{r balance-model}
```

```{r balance-plot}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 2.8
```

All three coefficients are close to zero and their confidence intervals
include zero; the $R^2$ is about $10^{-6}$. Girls and boys, and children
with high or low attendance and grades, met partners of the same expected
rank.

```{r balance-save}
```

# Figure 2: four layers of one classroom

Figure 2 shows, in one small classroom (9 children), the four networks the
analysis combines:

- **A. Friendship**: who named whom as a best friend. Green arrows are
  mutual friendships; blue arrows are one-sided.
- **B. Popularity** and **C. non-popularity**: who named whom as popular or
  as not popular. Social Rank is computed from these two layers.
- **D. Tokens**: every transfer in the game, darker for more tokens.

The same child keeps the same position in all four layers, so one can follow
how a child who is central in one layer fares in the others.

```{r sociogram-packages}
```

```{r sociogram-data}
```

To draw the four panels, we first fix one position for each child, computed
on the network that joins all four layers.

```{r sociogram-layout}
```

A small function draws one layer; it is called four times.

```{r sociogram-function}
```

Node size is the number of nominations received in A–C and the number of
tokens received in D.

```{r sociogram-panels}
#| fig-width: 5
#| fig-height: 11
```

# Figure 3: the exchanges behind the regressions

Table 1 summarizes the rank gradient in one number per sample. Figure 3 shows
the data behind it, in three columns, separately for non-friends (row I),
mutual friends (row II) and one-sided friendships (row III):

- **A. What pairs exchange.** For each pair, the two transfers (what $i$
  sent to $j$ and what $j$ sent to $i$) form one cell of an 11 × 11 grid. The
  heatmap shows the share of pairs in each cell. Since the order of the two
  children does not matter, the grid is folded into a triangle. Outlined
  regions mark low or no cooperation, very unequal exchanges, and full
  mutual cooperation (both send 10).
- **B. Tokens sent and received along the rank gap.** Average tokens sent
  (rhombi) and received (squares), in seven equal-width bins of the Social
  Rank GAP; the area between the two curves is the Cooperation GAP.
- **C. The Cooperation GAP along the rank gap.** The difference itself,
  from the observed data (solid) and from the null-model filtered data
  (semi-transparent; see the first page).

```{r fig3-packages}
```

## Panel A: what pairs exchange

```{r heatmap-data}
```

```{r heatmap-plot}
#| fig-width: 4
#| fig-height: 3.5
```

## Panels B and C: exchanges along the Social Rank GAP

Each child counts once. For each child we average her exchanges with the
partners in the group and take the median rank gap of those partners. The
children are then grouped into seven equal-width bins of that median rank
gap, and each point is the average across the children of a bin, with a 95%
confidence interval.

```{r binned-data}
```

```{r panel-b-plot}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
```

```{r panel-c-plot}
#| fig-width: 3.5
#| fig-height: 3
```

Among non-friends, the two curves cross: a child who meets a higher-ranked
classmate (left side) sends more than she receives; one who meets a
lower-ranked classmate (right side) receives more than she sends. So the
Cooperation GAP rises from negative to positive. Among mutual friends both
curves are higher (more giving overall) and they nearly overlap, so the
Cooperation GAP stays close to zero along the whole range.

```{r numbers-asymmetric}
```

**A rank read off the game.** Instead of nominations, rank can be computed
from the token network itself (PageRank on who gives to whom). This block
correlates that behavioral rank with the nomination-based Social Rank
(SI Section 9 has the full analysis).


and not popular, and the time between consecutive decisions.
